answer:
FINAL RESULT — headline proportion: 38/97 = 0.392 (39.2%)

(a) HEADLINE (exact recipe): dataset `meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv`; filter `project == "rpp"` (dictionary: rpp = Psychology) → 97 rows, all effect-type-level replication rows, `drop == True` rows retained; field `seniority.r` (most senior author of the replication team); numerator = rows where `seniority.r` ∈ {"Assistant", "Assistant Professor"} → 38. 38/97 = 0.3918, 39.2% (Wilson 95% CI 30.1%–49.1%). No joins, no recoding, zero missing values in `seniority.r`.

Full rpp seniority.r distribution: Associate Professor 24 (24.7%), Assistant Professor 23 (23.7%), Professor 19 (19.6%), Researcher 16 (16.5%), Assistant 15 (15.5%). Junior ranks therefore make up 39.2%, versus only 19.6% full professors.

(b) SENSITIVITY TABLE (all executed in analysis/final_proportion.py)
| variant | n | junior | proportion | 95% CI |
| HEADLINE rpp, all rows, seniority.r | 97 | 38 | 39.2% | 30.1–49.1% |
| unique original studies (title-level) | 95 | 38 | 40.0% | 30.7–50.1% |
| drop == False only | 90 | 36 | 40.0% | 30.5–50.3% |
| conditioned on success replicated==1 | 35 | 16 | 45.7% | 30.5–61.8% |
| replicated==1 & drop==False | 31 | 16 | 51.6% | 34.8–68.0% |
| conditioned on failure replicated==0 | 62 | 22 | 35.5% | 24.7–47.9% |
| junior incl. Associate Professor | 97 | 62 | 63.9% | 54.0–72.8% |
| junior = any non-full-professor (+Researcher) | 97 | 78 | 80.4% | 71.4–87.1% |
| field swap: seniority.o (original authors) | 97 | 0 | 0.0% | 0.0–3.8% |
| scope rpp+ml1+ml3 (coding artifact, not an answer) | 909 | 38 | 4.2% | 3.1–5.7% |
Definitional threshold matters most (39.2% → 63.9% → 80.4%); denominator/unit choices move it by ≤12 points and the headline is stable at ~39–40%.

(c) HYPOTHESIS / FINDING (study-level wording, as directed)
"In the Psychology replication project (project == 'rpp'), roughly two of every five replicated studies — 38 of 97, i.e. 39.2% (95% CI 30.1–49.1%) — were led by a junior professor, defined as an 'Assistant' or 'Assistant Professor' being the most senior author on the replication team (`seniority.r`). Junior ranks thus outnumber full Professors as lead replication investigators (39.2% vs 19.6%), with Associate Professors (24.7%) and Researchers (16.5%) accounting for the rest. This is a study-level proportion of the single recorded most senior author per replication, not an author-level share of all replication authors, since the database records exactly one seniority value per study. Junior leadership is not significantly associated with replication success (junior share 16/35 = 45.7% among successful replications vs 22/62 = 35.5% among failures; chi-square p = 0.44, Fisher p = 0.39), so the 39.2% composition figure should not be read as a success-conditioned statistic."

(d) CAVEATS
- `seniority.r` is documented as "Most senior author in the original paper", which I treat as a documentation copy-paste error: it disagrees with `seniority.o` on 79.4% of rpp rows (agreement 20.6%) and varies independently of original-author rank. If it truly duplicated `seniority.o`, the junior proportion would be 0/97, which is implausible given the 23 "Assistant Professor" and 15 "Assistant" values.
- `seniority.r` is coded "Professor" for every ml1 (592), ml3 (220) and ee (18) row — an uninformative default coding — so the estimate does NOT generalize beyond the Psychology (rpp) project; the 4.2% "all psychology projects" figure is an artifact of that default, not a competing answer.
- The source coding distinguishes "Assistant" from "Assistant Professor"; whether these are genuinely distinct ranks cannot be verified from these two files. "Assistant" may denote a non-professorial assistant-level rank, in which case a strictly professorial reading would give 23/97 = 23.7% (Assistant Professor only).
- 7 rpp rows carry the source `drop == True` exclusion flag and 2 rows lack replication effect sizes; retaining them (as directed) moves the estimate by 0.8 points.
- 97 rows correspond to 95 unique original studies (2 originals replicated on both a main effect and an interaction); using the study level gives 40.0%.

Executed artifacts: analysis/final_proportion.py (headline + sensitivities + diagnostics), analysis/final_report.txt (console record), plus the earlier analysis/inspect_seniority.py and analysis/inspection_summary.txt.

payload.hypothesis: In the Psychology replication project (project == 'rpp'), 39.2% of replicated studies (38 of 97) were led by a junior professor - an 'Assistant' or 'Assistant Professor' as the most senior author on the replication team (seniority.r) - roughly twice the share led by full Professors (19.6%), with Associate Professors (24.7%) and Researchers (16.5%) making up the remainder. This is a study-level proportion of the single recorded most senior replication author per study, not an author-level share. Junior leadership is not significantly associated with replication success (45.7% among successful vs 35.5% among failed replications, Fisher p = 0.39), so the ~39% figure describes who conducts replications rather than a success-conditioned composition; it applies only to the Psychology (rpp) project because seniority.r is coded 'Professor' for every Many Labs 1/3 and Experimental Economics row.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows x 57 cols; the only staged file containing seniority fields - the replication-success file has none and was used only to corroborate that the label 'Psychology' corresponds to rpp via surname overlap). Filtered project == 'rpp' (97 rows, one per original-study x effect-type, drop==True rows retained per directive). Used seniority.r as the replication-team seniority field (seniority.o contains zero junior values within rpp). Computed the primary proportion as the share of rows with seniority.r in {'Assistant','Assistant Professor'} = 38/97 = 0.3918, with a Wilson 95% CI (30.1-49.1%). Reported labelled sensitivities for unit (95 unique original studies), exclusion flag (drop==False, 36/90), success conditioning (replicated==1, 16/35; and 16/31 excluding drop rows), junior threshold (+Associate 62/97; any non-full-professor 78/97), field swap (seniority.o, 0/97) and broader psychology scope (38/909, documented coding artifact). Added diagnostics: full seniority distribution, seniority.o/.r agreement (0.206), junior x replicated chi-square/Fisher tests, missingness (0 in both seniority fields). Code: analysis/final_proportion.py; console record: analysis/final_report.txt (earlier inspection pass: analysis/inspect_seniority.py, analysis/inspection_summary.txt).
